# *t*-Tests as a Linear Model


## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model

We can specify a *t*-test as a linear model.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Our goal with *t*-tests is to compare means.

$H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ aka $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
We can estimate the overall mean of the outcome with an intercept-only model, where $\beta_0$ is the intercept.

$y = \beta_0 + \epsilon$

Then, we can add a slope term $\beta_1$ to represent the difference in means between groups.

$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{group} + \epsilon$
:::
::::


## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model

Together, these parameters contain us the same information as a *t*-test.

For example, in an experiment, if the control group is coded $\text{group}_\text{control} = 0$ and the treatment group is coded $\text{group}_\text{control} = 1$,

::: subpoint
○ $\beta_0 =$ mean of control group
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\beta_1 =$ difference in means between control group and treatment group
:::

::: subpoint
○ $\beta_0 + \beta_1 =$ mean of treatment group
:::



# Bayesian *t*-Tests


## Bayesian Inference

So far, we've been working with the frequentist statistical framework, Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST).

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Frequentist**

In NHST, we speak only about *likelihoods*. The probability that we would have observed our data $D$ (or more extreme data) given some null hypothesis parameter $\theta$

E.g., the probability that we would observe a mean difference on a test of $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$ points given the true mean difference in the population is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 0$.

$P(D | \theta)$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Bayesian**

What we as researchers are often more interested in is the probability that a parameter $\theta$ is the true parameter given data $D$ we have observed.

E.g., given that we have observed a mean difference of $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$, what is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 0$? What is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$?

$P(\theta | D)$
:::
::::


## Bayesian Inference

In order to get $P(\theta | D)$, we need Bayes' Rule. 

$$ P(\theta | D) = \frac{ P(\theta) P(D | \theta) }{ P(D) } $$

::: subpoint
○ $P(\theta | D) =$ *posterior* distribution, this is what we want to create!
:::

::: subpoint
○ $P(\theta)$ *prior* distribution, information we know about $\theta$ before seeing $D$
:::

::: subpoint
○ $P(D | \theta)$ likelihood, the same as before
:::

::: subpoint
○ $P(D)$ scaling term, brings everything back down to probability scale. Makes Bayes analytic calulations mathematically challenging / impossible! 
:::

::: fragment
Motivates *sampling* from the posterior distribution, instead of calculating it.
:::


## Getting to the Posterior

Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false

# I made the original plot; gave to Claude to help with the 
# labelling and annotating.
n <- 10
k <- 2

a <- 8
b <- 6

x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)

curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x, y = dbeta(x, a, b), curve = "Prior"),
  tibble(x, y = choose(n, k) * x^k * (1 - x)^(n - k) * 8, curve = "Likelihood"),
  tibble(x, y = dbeta(x, a + k, b + n - k), curve = "Posterior")
) |>
  mutate(hjust = recode_values(
    curve,
    "Prior" ~ 0.1,
    "Posterior" ~ 0.7,
    "Likelihood" ~ 0.36
    
  ))

# where to point the arrow: the posterior's peak
post_mode <- (a + k - 1) / (a + b + n - 2)
post_peak <- dbeta(post_mode, a + k, b + n - k)

just_prior <- curves |>
  filter(curve == "Prior")

just_prior |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, label = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geomtextpath::geom_textline(
    aes(color = curve),
    linewidth = 1,
    hjust = just_prior$hjust,            # position of label along each curve (0-1)
    vjust = -0.2,           # sit just above the line
    size = 5
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dotted", Likelihood = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "steelblue", Likelihood = "#D98282", Posterior = "#8C7AAE")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


## Getting to the Posterior

Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
just_prior_and_likelihood <- curves |>
  filter(curve == "Prior" | curve == "Likelihood")

just_prior_and_likelihood |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, label = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geomtextpath::geom_textline(
    aes(color = curve),
    linewidth = 1,
    hjust = just_prior_and_likelihood$hjust,            # position of label along each curve (0-1)
    vjust = -0.2,           # sit just above the line
    size = 5
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dotted", Likelihood = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "steelblue", Likelihood = "#D98282", Posterior = "#8C7AAE")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Getting to the Posterior

Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$.

<!-- But most of the time, $P(\theta | D)$ is too complex to solve analytically.  -->

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
ggplot(curves, aes(x, y, label = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geomtextpath::geom_textline(
    aes(color = curve),
    linewidth = 1,
    hjust = curves$hjust,            # position of label along each curve (0-1)
    vjust = -0.2,           # sit just above the line
    size = 5
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dotted", Likelihood = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "steelblue", Likelihood = "#D98282", Posterior = "#8C7AAE")) +
  annotate("curve",
           x = post_mode + 0.225, xend = post_mode + 0.08,
           y = post_peak * 0.97, yend = post_peak * 0.92,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           linewidth = 0.6, color = scales::col_darker("#8C7AAE", 30)) +
  annotate("text",
           x = post_mode + 0.25, y = post_peak * 0.94,
           label = "Can be difficult or impossible\nto analytically calculate" |>
             str_wrap(25),
           hjust = 0, size = 4.5, lineheight = 0.9, 
           color = scales::col_darker("#8C7AAE", 30)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Getting to the Posterior

How can we sample from posterior distributions? We can use a *probabalistic programming language*.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](https://mc-stan.org/docs/img/logo_tm.png)
:::

::: {.column width="66%"}
*Stan* is an open-source probabalistic programming language that's widely used to write Bayesian models.

It has a well-developed, user-friendly R interface called `rstanarm`, which we will use!

::: subpoint-narrow
○ Means we can start to work with Bayesian models without having to lean the Stan language itself
:::
:::
::::


## Bayesian *t*-Tests

A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package!

```{r}
# install.packages("rstanarm")
library(rstanarm)

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

filtered_mpg <- mpg |>
  filter(when_any(cyl == 4, cyl == 8)) |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))
```


## Bayesian *t*-Tests

A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package!

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
freq_t_test <- t.test(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg)
freq_t_test
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
                         family = "gaussian")
summary(bayes_t_test)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
                         family = "gaussian", refresh = 0)
summary(bayes_t_test)
```
:::
::::


## Bayesian *t*-Tests

A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package!

:::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
`summary()` function contains lots of information about the model:

::: subpoint-narrow
○ `Estimates`: means, SDs, and quantiles (can specify with `probs`) for each parameter.
:::

::: subpoint-narrow
○ `Fit Diagnostics`: `mean_PPD` mean of the posterior distribution of the outcome. If `mean_PPD` is very different from what you'd expect the mean of the outcome variable to be, may be an indicator of something being wrong. 
:::

::: subpoint-narrow
○ `MCMC Diagnostics`: Diagnostics for the Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler (more on this later).
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
                         family = "gaussian")
summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
                         family = "gaussian", refresh = 0)
summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```
:::
::::


## Bayesian *t*-Tests

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
prior_summary(bayes_t_test)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`\{rstanarm\}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model.

The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used.
:::
::::


## Full Model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{highway MPG}_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{cylinders}_i + \epsilon_i && \text{likelihood: a linear model} \\
\beta_0 &\sim N(24, 17) && \text{prior for intercept} \\
\beta_1 &\sim N(0, 8.6) && \text{prior for slope} \\
\epsilon &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.15)  && \text{prior for residual variance}
\end{aligned}
$$


## Visualizing Results

The `bayesplot` package provides many helpful functions for plotting results of a Bayesian model.

```{r}
# install.packages("bayesplot")
library(bayesplot)
```

## Prior Implications

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Given that the distribution of the outcome following just the priors includes negative values for highway MPG, maybe we can afford to narrow them a bit!

And maybe we want to be a little more skeptical of large effects, so we can narrow the prior on the slope, too.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center
t_test_from_prior_only <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
  family = "gaussian", refresh = 0,
  prior_PD = T
)
ppc_dens_overlay_grouped(
  y = filtered_mpg$hwy, 
  yrep = posterior_predict(t_test_from_prior_only, draws = 50),
  group = filtered_mpg$cyl
)
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
t_test_from_prior_only <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
  family = "gaussian", refresh = 0,
  prior_PD = T
)
ppc_dens_overlay_grouped(
  y = filtered_mpg$hwy, 
  yrep = posterior_predict(t_test_from_prior_only, draws = 50),
  group = filtered_mpg$cyl
)
```
:::

::::


## Changing Priors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Original Model**
```{r}
prior_summary(bayes_t_test)
```
:::

::: {.column style="font-size:80%" width="50%"}
`\{{rstanarm}\}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model.

The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used.

We can choose to specify a prior on the *z*-scale (`autoscale = T`) or as-is (default) (example on next slide).
:::
::::


## Changing Priors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Original Model**
```{r}
prior_summary(bayes_t_test)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
  prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T),
  prior_intercept = normal(24, 15),
  family = "gaussian"
)
summary(bayes_t_test_v2, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
  prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T),
  prior_intercept = normal(24, 15),
  family = "gaussian"
)
summary(bayes_t_test_v2, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```
:::
::::


## Prior Implications

:::: {.columns}

```{r}
ppc_dens_overlay_grouped(
```

# Diagnostics


## Diagnostics

Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$.

But most of the time, $P(\theta | D)$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models by drawing **samples** from the posterior with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
n <- 10
k <- 2

a <- 8
b <- 6

x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)

curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x, y = dbeta(x, a, b), curve = "Prior"),
  tibble(x, y = choose(n, k) * x^k * (1 - x)^(n - k) * 8, curve = "Likelihood"),
  tibble(x, y = dbeta(x, a + k, b + n - k), curve = "Posterior")
) |>
  mutate(hjust = recode_values(
    curve,
    "Prior" ~ 0.1,
    "Posterior" ~ 0.7,
    "Likelihood" ~ 0.36
    
  ))

post_mode <- (a + k - 1) / (a + b + n - 2)
post_peak <- dbeta(post_mode, a + k, b + n - k)

just_prior_and_likelihood <- curves |>
  filter(curve == "Prior" | curve == "Likelihood")

n_samples <- 4000

set.seed(2)
posterior_samples <- tibble(
  t = 1:n_samples,
  x = rbeta(n_samples, a + k, b + n - k)
)

base_plot <- just_prior_and_likelihood |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, label = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geomtextpath::geom_textline(
    aes(color = curve),
    linewidth = 1,
    hjust = just_prior_and_likelihood$hjust,            # position of label along each curve (0-1)
    vjust = -0.2,           # sit just above the line
    size = 5
  ) +
  annotate("curve",
           x = post_mode + 0.225, xend = post_mode + 0.08,
           y = post_peak * 0.97, yend = post_peak * 0.92,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           linewidth = 0.6, color = scales::col_darker("#8C7AAE", 30)) +
  annotate("text",
           x = post_mode + 0.25, y = post_peak * 0.94,
           label = "Can be difficult or impossible\nto analytically calculate" |>
             str_wrap(25),
           hjust = 0, size = 4.5, lineheight = 0.9, 
           color = scales::col_darker("#8C7AAE", 30)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dotted", Likelihood = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "steelblue", Likelihood = "#D98282", Posterior = "#8C7AAE")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

post_col <- "#8C7AAE"

base_plot +
  geom_density(
    data = posterior_samples,   # density needs >= 2 points
    aes(x = x),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = post_col, color = post_col, alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = posterior_samples,
    aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = 0.2),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = scales::col_darker(post_col, 30), linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_none(),
         alpha = guide_none()) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, color = "grey40", hjust = 0.02),
        legend.position = "none")
```



## Diagnostics with Bayes

But most of the time, $P(\theta | D)$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).

[The job of MCMC is to explore and sample from the posterior probability distribution $P(\theta | D)$ for all $\theta$ at a rate proportional to each probability.]{.fragment}

[So, after many MCMC samples, we end up with a density distribution of samples with height matching $P(\theta | D)$, and we can use those samples to make inferences about our parameters and outcomes!]{.fragment}

::: {.subpoint .fragment}
○ E.g., we believe there is a 90% chance the difference in highway MPG between four- and eight-cylinder cars is within the interval [`r posterior_interval(bayes_t_test)["cyl8", ] |> round(2) |> paste(collapse = ", ")`].
:::

[But, all this hinges on the MCMC sampler---we have to check it for evidence that it *sampled well*.]{.fragment}


## Looking at the Samples

Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled!

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[This is called a *trace plot*. It shows the samplers' samples for each iteration it runs. Can you tell if this sampler sampled well?]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
scale_colors <-  c("steelblue", "#D98282", "#6BAE9D", "#8C7AAE")
x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors)
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
scale_colors <-  c("steelblue", "#D98282", "#6BAE9D", "#8C7AAE")
x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors)
```
:::
:::
:::

[Looking at traceplots cannot guarantee the sampler is **correctly** sampling from the distribution, but if we run multiple *chains* (separate runs of MCMC, each doing their own thing independently), we can at least check if the sampler is sampling **consistently**.]{.fragment}


[Good! They look like "fuzzy caterpillars".]{.fragment}


## Trace Rank Plots

These are called "trace rank" plots. They're very similar to trace plots, except they *order* the samples in magnitude. Want to see all chains (colors) equally represented across the x-axis.

It's mostly personal preference, but these are sometimes easier to see bad chains.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 12
mcmc_rank_overlay(bayes_t_test_v2)
```

[What does a bad chain look like?]{.fragment}

## Rhat

Looking at traceplots is great, but it's also helpful to have a numerical measure of how well the chains mixed. Especially when you have lots of parameters, not just three.

[Rhat ($\hat{R}$, read "R-hat") is a measure of convergence among different MCMC *chains*.]{.fragment}

[The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains.]{.fragment}


## Rhat Visualized: Bad

The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)
n_samples <- 500
d <- tibble(chain = 1:4) |>
  mutate(
    chain_mu = c(3, 3.3, 2.3, 5),
    samples = map(
      chain_mu, \(chain_mu) tibble(
        rep = 1:n_samples, 
        sin_x = sin(1:n_samples)^100,
        x = sin_x + rnorm(n_samples, chain_mu, 0.3)
      ) 
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(samples)

chain_means <- d |>
  summarize(.by = chain, x = mean(x))

d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rep, y = x, color = factor(chain), group = chain)) +
  geom_line() +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_none(NULL),
         color = guide_none(),
         fill = guide_none()) +
  scale_x_continuous("Rep", limits = c(-50, n_samples + 50), breaks = seq(0, 500, 100)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1.2, 6)) +
  theme_classic()
```
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

:::
::::

In practice, you want to see $\hat{R}$ values less than 1.01.

```{r}
summary(bayes_t_test_v2)
```

```{r}
summary(bayes_t_test_v2)[, "Rhat"]
```

## Effective Sample Size (ESS)

In order to closely approximate the posterior ($P(\theta | D)$, the point of this all!), we need to make sure we have a large number of MCMC samples.

But one issue: the samples within a chain are **not** independent samples.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors)
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) +
  scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors)
```
:::


:::

::: {.column width="66%"}
Do you see how they follow each other around?

ESS accounts for that *autocorrelation*. No hard and fast rule, but might be concerned if ESS is lower than 200 or lower than 10% of your total samples.
:::
::::

## Effective Sample Size (ESS)

Bulk and Tail ESS tell you about your effective sample size in the center (bulk) of the distribution and the tails of the distribution. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
post_col  <- "#8C7AAE"
annot_col <- scales::col_darker(post_col, 30)

# Posterior quantiles for placing the annotations
tail_x <- qbeta(0.99, a + k, b + n - k)
tail_y <- dbeta(tail_x, a + k, b + n - k)

base_plot <- just_prior_and_likelihood |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, label = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geomtextpath::geom_textline(
    aes(color = curve),
    linewidth = 1,
    hjust = just_prior_and_likelihood$hjust,
    vjust = -0.2,
    size = 5
  ) +
  # Bulk annotation
  annotate("curve",
           x = post_mode - 0.15, xend = post_mode - 0.1,
           y = post_peak * 0.76, yend = post_peak * 0.68,
           curvature = -0.25,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           linewidth = 0.6, color = annot_col) +
  annotate("text",
           x = post_mode - 0.34, y = post_peak * 0.75,
           label = str_wrap("Do I have enough samples of the posterior here?", 22),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 4.5, lineheight = 0.9,
           color = annot_col) +
  # Tail annotation
  annotate("curve",
           x = tail_x + 0.12, xend = tail_x + 0.005,
           y = 1.5, yend = tail_y + 0.05,
           curvature = 0.25,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           linewidth = 0.6, color = annot_col) +
  annotate("text",
           x = tail_x + 0.13, y = 1.55,
           label = "How about here?",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 4.5, lineheight = 0.9,
           color = annot_col) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dotted", Likelihood = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Prior = "steelblue", Likelihood = "#D98282", Posterior = "#8C7AAE")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 4.1), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

base_plot +
  geom_density(
    data = posterior_samples,
    aes(x = x),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = post_col, color = post_col, alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = posterior_samples,
    aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = 0.2),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = scales::col_darker(post_col, 30), linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.35
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_none(), alpha = guide_none()) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, color = "grey40", hjust = 0.02),
        legend.position = "none")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}

posterior::summarise_draws(bayes_t_test_v2, 
                           "mean", "sd", 
                           "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
```

## Warnings

[Stan documentation on warnings](https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html)

[`{rstanarm}` documentation on troubleshooting`](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/articles/rstanarm.html#troubleshooting){preview-link="}

Things to try...

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Rhat or ESS too low?**

Try increasing the number of samples (`iter`, default is 1000 for each of four chains).
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Divergent transitions?**

Increase `adapt_delta` towards 1 (default is `0.95`)
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Max treedepth exceeded?**

If everything else is good, probably fine. Otherwise, try increasing `max_treedepth` (default is 15). Add to `control` argument (`control = list(max_treedepth = 16)`).
:::
::::


## Bayes Factors

Comparing models to each other. Here, an intercept-only model to a slope-and-intercept model.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| cache: true
# install.packages("bayestestR")
# install.packages("bridgesampling")
bayes_t_test_v0 <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ 1, data = filtered_mpg,
  prior_intercept = normal(24, 15),
  family = "gaussian",
  diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", 
                               "bayes_t_test_v0.csv")
)
bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm(
  hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg,
  prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T),
  prior_intercept = normal(24, 15),
  family = "gaussian",
  diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", 
                               "bayes_t_test_v2.csv")
)

bayes_factor <- bayestestR::bayesfactor_models(bayes_t_test_v0, 
                                               bayes_t_test_v2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
bayes_factor
```

We can say the model with the slope term is $9.44\times10^{33}$ (very large!) times as likely as the model without.
